2104.description: Big Bend Cares seeks funding to retire the remaining mortgage on the Care Point Health & Wellness Center, a critical regional hub providing integrated primary care, dental, behavioral health, HIV specialty care, pharmacy, and prevention services to uninsured, underinsured, and medically vulnerable residents across the Big Bend. Eliminating this facility debt unlocks essential operating dollars, allowing Care Point to dramatically expand service capacity, reduce wait times, strengthen partnerships with local FQHCs, and stabilize the region’s strained safety-net system. This investment ensures that thousands of high-need residents can access timely, comprehensive, and coordinated healthcare in a single, patient-centered location—improving overall community health outcomes and long-term system resiliency.
2104.purpose: Eliminating the facility debt frees critical operating dollars to expand primary care, dental, behavioral health, and prevention services for uninsured and underserved patients. This investment strengthens Care Point’s capacity, reduces strain on regional FQHC partners, and creates a more balanced safety-net system that improves access and health outcomes across the Big Bend.
2104.activities: Retiring the Care Point facility debt frees critical operating funds to expand primary care, dental, behavioral health, pharmacy, prevention, and support services for uninsured and underserved patients. Funds enable increased appointments, reduced wait times, and strengthened regional safety-net capacity.
2104.direct_services: Expanded access to primary medical care, dental services, behavioral health counseling, pharmacy services, HIV care, prevention services, case management, care coordination, health education, and supportive services for uninsured, underinsured, and medically vulnerable residents across the Big Bend region.
2104.population: This project serves uninsured, underinsured, low-income, medically vulnerable individuals; people with HIV or at risk of HIV; persons with poor mental or physical health; homeless individuals; people with disabilities; high-school and college-age youth; justice-involved individuals; and other economically disadvantaged residents across the Big Bend region. Expected to be served: 800+ individuals annually.
2104.outcome: The expected outcome of this project is an expansion of primary care, dental, behavioral health, pharmacy, HIV care, and prevention services made possible by freeing operating dollars currently tied to facility debt. This investment will increase Care Point’s capacity, reduce patient wait times, improve physical and mental health outcomes, strengthen care coordination, and enhance the overall resilience of the regional safety-net system. These outcomes will be measured through electronic health record data evaluating visit volumes, clinical indicators, and patient retention; pharmacy dispensing and adherence metrics; behavioral health assessments including PHQ-9 and GAD-7 score changes; medi

2166.description: The Workforce Entrepreneurship Resource eXchange is a 100,000 square foot interdisciplinary facility representing a transformational new model for partnership where higher education and employers co-locate to spark discovery, strengthen workforce pipelines, and turn ideas into real-world impact. This facility will serve to expand workforce readiness, drive entrepreneurship, and accelerate partnerships that meet the state’s high-demand talent needs.
2166.purpose: The Workforce Entrepreneurship Resource eXchange will be a 100,000-square-foot interdisciplinary facility designed to serve as a bridge between UCF’s academic mission and its industry partners. This building will embody a transformational concept: the integration of higher education and industry under one roof. By co-locating students, faculty, and employers, the facility will accelerate knowledge transfer, promote hands-on learning, and support job creation in high-demand sectors.
2166.activities: The building will include active learning classrooms, flexible teaching labs, and hands-on maker spaces that prepare students to think creatively, solve problems collaboratively, and apply their skills in real-world contexts. An entrepreneurship incubator and industry collaboration suites will connect students directly with employers, fostering internship opportunities, applied research, and startup development. The model of UCF personnel sharing space with industry partners will enable new syne
2166.direct_services: In addition to 13(b), above, expanding applied learning capacity across multiple colleges; supporting small- and medium-sized businesses seeking university partnerships; creating a sustainable talent pipeline in engineering, computing, business, and emerging technologies; and providing a collaborative space where innovation leads directly to job growth and entrepreneurship.
2166.population: College and university students and faculty, regional engineering and high-tech government and industry partners, entrepreneurs of small- and medium-sized businesses. Over the course of years, hundreds of thousands of individuals are expected to be served.
2166.outcome: The Workforce Entrepreneurship Resource eXchange directly supports state priorities for workforce development and economic growth by: (1) increasing the number of graduates prepared for high-demand STEM and entrepreneurial fields; (2) strengthening collaboration between UCF and industry partners; (3) expanding internship and collaborative opportunities that translate into immediate employment, and (4) promoting technology transfer and new business formation through joint research and innovation.

2444.description: To build new classrooms, upgrade safety infrastructure, update gymnasium, and construct a multipurpose assembly facility, creating a secure and modern environment that supports education, recreation, and community engagement at the Gan Israel Florida Campus.
2444.purpose: Build new classrooms, upgrade safety infrastructure, update gymnasium, and construct a multipurpose assembly facility, creating a secure and modern environment that supports education, recreation, and community engagement.
2444.activities: Funds will support construction of modular classrooms, safety upgrades, and a multipurpose facility. Programs will offer academic enrichment, Judaic and arts learning, and summer camp activities.
2444.direct_services: The camp will serve children statewide by building shovel-ready modular classrooms, a multipurpose assembly facility, and upgrading the gymnasium—providing a safe, high-quality environment where children can learn and thrive during the summer months, supporting their continued educational growth throughout the year.
2444.population: The target population includes at-risk youth, grade school students, high school students, and university/college students, with an estimated 350 individuals expected to be served annually.
2444.outcome: The project will improve students’ educational readiness, social-emotional well-being, and overall safety by providing structured enrichment programs, upgraded facilities, and supportive learning environments. Participants will benefit from increased academic engagement, strengthened life skills, improved mental and physical health, and enhanced pathways toward long-term success. Outcomes will be measured through attendance tracking, pre- and post-program assessments, staff observation reports, participant and parent surveys.

2208.description: MACTown residents are ambulatory with underline medical conditions requiring strict diets and medication management. The funding requested would fund the installation of a new generator allowing individuals with I/DD to shelter in place and ensuring their safety in case of a natural disaster or emergency.
2208.purpose: Funds will be used for the hardening and security of MACtown Main Campus for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Scope includes re-roofing day training center, fixing of drainage issues on perimeter parking lot and install gas-powered emergency generator.
2208.activities: The replacement of and installation of gas-powered generator.
2208.direct_services: The funds requested are being used toward replacement of the gas generator and other improvements to the physical building.
2208.population: The residents current and future of MACTown.
2208.outcome: Life safety, security, and critical services for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

1825.description: This request is to purchase a second VACTOR truck to enhance the City’s ability to maintain its storm and sanitary sewer systems effectively.
1825.purpose: The City of Port Richey is seeking state funding for to purchase a second VACTOR truck to enhance the City’s ability to maintain its storm and sanitary sewer systems effectively.
1825.activities: Currently, the City operates with a single VACTOR truck, which is insufficient to manage the growing workload due to aging infrastructure, expanding service areas, and more frequent storm events. The existing truck is often over-utilized, leading to downtime for repairs and delayed response times for routine maintenance and urgent issues such as blockages and flooding.
1825.direct_services: A second VACTOR truck will allow the City to increase its maintenance capacity, extend the lifespan of the storm and sanitary sewer systems, and reduce the risks of localized flooding and sewer backups.
1825.outcome: It will also enable a more proactive maintenance schedule, improving service reliability and environmental compliance.

2396.description: The program will advance the implementation of a preventive mental health wellness initiative for Jacksonville’s Historic Eastside community (HEC). The program will target representative HEC households with community interventions that promote mental health through education about early detection and wellness. Services will be differentiated for the unique needs of HEC elderly, families, and youth to raise awareness of, and decrease, mental health risk factors.
2396.purpose: The specific goal accomplished by these services is to strengthen the mental health and emotional well-being of residents in urban communities by increasing early identification of mental health needs, expanding access to timely support and crisis intervention, and building a coordinated, community-based network that improves awareness, reduces stigma, and enhances collaboration between residents and the professionals who serve them.
2396.activities: Key services 1) education/awareness of mental health risk factors for urban community contexts 2) increase residents’ screening/early detection of mental health issues 3) increase access to counseling/crisis intervention services, and 4) improve collaboration between residents and educators/healthcare providers/community leaders who provide mental health and related services to communities.
2396.direct_services: Monthly workshops/seminars on mental health (MH) awareness/help-seeking that emphasize self-advocacy and community networking; regular MH screenings collaboration with schools/community agencies/healthcare providers; trainings on locating and accessing counseling services; group support counseling; continuing education that engages households as partners in improving community wellness/outcomes
2396.population: The target population for this project includes elderly persons, individuals experiencing poor mental health, economically disadvantaged residents, at-risk youth, people experiencing homelessness, and students across grade school, high school, and college settings.
2396.outcome: The expected benefits of this project include improved mental health, enhanced physical well-being, enriched cultural experiences that strengthen community identity, and improvements in the quality of education through increased awareness, access to resources, and coordinated support systems and diversion from Criminal/ Juvenile Justice System

2519.description: Nations Against Bullying (NAB) seeks funding to operate a regional bullying-prevention and mental-health support initiative across Central Florida. The program delivers school-based anti-bullying workshops, therapeutic counseling, tutoring support, a 24/7 youth hotline, parental guidance, and bilingual social-media prevention campaigns. Funds will support program staff, contracted therapists, outreach activities, office rent, materials, and operational costs. The project will serve more than 800 students and families annually, with expanded reach through social-media education
2519.purpose: To reduce bullying and cyberbullying incidents among Central Florida youth by providing prevention workshops, therapeutic intervention, tutoring support, and 24/7 crisis hotline services, while promoting emotional well-being, academic success, and safe school environments.
2519.activities: Anti-bullying school workshops for students, parents, and staff; Therapeutic counseling and mental-health intervention; Tutoring and academic reinforcement for victims; crisis hotline for youth and families; Bilingual social-media prevention campaigns; Case management and referrals to long-term care resources.
2519.direct_services: Individual therapy and crisis intervention; Emotional support via hotline; Academic tutoring; Peer support groups; Parental training; Safety education and cyberbullying prevention; Service coordination with schools, mental-health agencies, and families.
2519.population: At-risk youth: Economically disadvantaged families; Persons with poor mental health; Grade-school and high-school students; Victims of crime (bullying, harassment, cyberbullying); Minority, Hispanic, immigrant, ESL populations, 800–1,200 individuals annually.
2519.outcome: Outcome Specific Measure Methodology 1.Improve mental health.70% show reduced anxiety/depression indicatorsPre-/post-psychological assessments 2.Improve education 60% show academic improvement Tutor progress tracking + school data 3. Protect the general public25% reduction in bullying incidents School reports, hotline analytics Enhance cultural inclusion100% bilingual workshops deliveredAttendance logs

2001.description: Requested funds would be used to purchase new infusion pumps, system wide, that will integrate with the Epic Electronic Health Records System, as well as the MyChart Bedside TV service for patients. The infusion pumps will allow for more accurate and timely medication delivery, and faster documentation. MyChart offers patients an interactive experience with informative videos on their care team and vital information regarding their care, schedule, medications, instructions, reminders, etc.
2001.purpose: Upgraded infusion pumps will enable faster documentation of medication administrations; minimize transcription errors associated with manual entry; promote accurate capture of data. MyChart Bedside TV will offer improved access to information related to care and recovery for all patients.
2001.activities: Physician orders for patient medication will be directly sent to the infusion pump, therefore allowing for quicker administration of the medications, better documentation, minimized errors, and less clinician time spent on data entry and more with the patients. MyChart Bedside TV offers patients an interactive experience that will provide access at their bedside to information on their care team, condition, medications, instructions, and recovery.
2001.direct_services: Enable faster documentation of medication administrations; minimize transcription errors associated with manual entry; promote accurate capture of data; etc. MyChart Bedside TV offers patients an interactive experience that will provide access at their bedside to information on their care team, condition, medications, instructions, and recovery.
2001.population: All citizens of Volusia County who need medical attention provided within the Halifax Hospital Medical Center system.
2001.outcome: Improved patient outcomes, reduced costs, lives saves. Comparison of before and after outcomes.

1879.description: Reef Relief is seeking funds to expand and enhance our Coral Reef Conservation Program (CRCP). Funds will be used to broaden the reach of our educational programs. The Discover Coral Reefs School Program, spring and summer programs will raise awareness and educate consumers, providing educational messaging to students, adults, and tourism in Florida.
1879.purpose: We are requesting funding to support our Coral Reef Youth Education Program. This program places a special focus on youth education as an important, initial step in saving endangered marine ecosystems through two main components, our Discover Coral Reefs School Program (DCRSP) and our Coral Camp for Kids program.
1879.activities: Our Discover Coral Reefs School Program offers over a dozen marine science topics taught in interactive classroom presentations supplemented with question-and-answer sessions and related activities. Reef Relief also offers a unique educational opportunity through our Coral Camp for Kids and Reef Explorer Coral Camp Programs.
1879.direct_services: Students Pre-Kindergarten through graduate level will be empowered to make informed decisions. They will gain experiences and snorkel skills from visiting the coral reef. As well as life skills regarding decision making, critical thinking, and resource partitioning. Residents will experience better quality of life from decreased pollution. Tourism will have higher quality experience elevating the
1879.population: The Discover Coral Reefs School Program, spring and summer programs, target students aged Pre-Kindergarten through graduate level. While we will target approximately 12,000 students worldwide through in person and virtual learning, there will be a special emphasis on students, adults, and tourists, specifically those located in Florida counties directly impacted by the Florida Barrier Reef.
1879.outcome: Participants in the Discover Coral Reefs Middle School Program and spring and summer programs are pre and post tested. Every year, we aim to stay in line with or increase the retention rates for both programs. This is a way to not only gauge the success of our programs, but to determine the effectiveness of our teachings. We are also starting to see program alumni and students graduate and go on to pursue marine conservation fields.

2167.description: Yeshua El Pan De Vida, Inc. (YBOL) seeks funding to complete a drainage and flood mitigation project that will address ongoing flooding on our property and nearby homes in the Azalea Park community. The project will connect our site to the Orange County stormwater system and install an underground drainage line to direct water to existing storm wells, creating a permanent solution that improves safety, protects property, and strengthens community resilience. These improvements will support proper water flow in an area with limited drainage infrastructure. The project will also reduce recurring flooding that impacts residents, streets, and community access during major storm events.
2167.purpose: The funds will support construction of a permanent drainage and flood mitigation system to resolve ongoing flooding affecting Yeshua El Pan De Vida, Inc. and the surrounding Azalea Park community. The project will connect the property to the Orange County stormwater system and install an underground drainage line to redirect stormwater away from nearby homes and streets, reducing property damage and improving public safety. This will provide a reliable, long-term infrastructure solution for the
2167.activities: Activities include engineering design, land preparation, installation of underground drainage infrastructure, and connection to existing storm wells to create a functional and sustainable drainage system. The project will also include grading and site improvements to direct water flow, as well as inspections and testing to ensure proper capacity and long-term performance. These activities will result in a fully integrated system that reliably manages stormwater for both the property and surround
2167.direct_services: The project will directly reduce flooding for nearby residents, improve street accessibility during storms, enhance public safety, and protect homes and community facilities in the surrounding Azalea Park area. It will also provide more reliable access for emergency services during severe weather events. In addition, the improved drainage will help prevent recurring property damage, creating a saf
2167.population: The project serves approximately 150 individuals within the Yeshua El Pan De Vida, Inc. community, as well as residents living along Hibiscus Road, Cadenza Street, Dahlia Drive, Marigold Avenue, and the broader Azalea Park area. The improvements will also benefit surrounding neighborhoods that experience flooding and access challenges during major storms. This includes homeowners, renters, and families who rely on these streets for daily travel. The project will further support safer conditions
2167.outcome: The expected outcome is a significant reduction in storm-related flooding on the Yeshua El Pan De Vida, Inc. property and surrounding streets. Success will be measured by monitoring stormwater flow, reduced flood occurrences during heavy rain events, improved road passability, and feedback from residents confirming fewer flooding impacts. The project is also expected to decrease property damage and lower public safety risks during major storms, with long-term performance evaluated through post-storm inspections.

2407.description: The current Orange City (City) Fire Station No. 68 is located on City-owned property in a retrofitted manufactured home that houses is operations and bunkers. The City has previously contracted for architectural schematics and design for a new hurricane-hardened Fire Station, which is currently completed to 30% design. This funding request will help facilitate bringing architectural and design to 100%.
2407.purpose: Funding a new, storm-hardened Fire facility to provide support for an emergency operations base will ensure public safety operations are protected and remain viable in situations of hazardous weather and disaster events, and allow emergency staff to properly respond to the community needs before, during, and after hurricanes and other disaster related events that impact the City and local area.
2407.activities: Fire Station No. 68 serves the Orange City commercial corridor and growing multi-family units in the south area of the city. The funding will facilitate architectural and design being completed from 30% design to 100% design.
2407.direct_services: Ensure the Fire division has a secure and functional facility from which to administer disaster and emergency public services to over 14,000 citizens of Orange City.
2407.population: All estimated 14,882 permanent residents of the city, as well as transient business visitors of around 35,000 per day who come to Orange City every day to utilize our medical services, retail shopping, and restaurant outlets.
2407.outcome: The most critical benefit will be to provide a hurricane-hardened Fire Station that will ensure the safety of emergency personnel so they can effectively respond to weather related and disasters during and after an incident, in addition to regular emergency calls.

2412.description: The project is located in an older area that saw extensive flooding in Hurricanes Ian & Milton. It includes the construction of two new stormwater ponds, along with new pipes and inlets to route the stormwater to the new ponds, and the addition of a backflow prevention device to an existing outfall beneath the Florida East Coast (FEC) railroad tracks. This will help relieve flooding for about 50 homes in the immediate area built mostly in the 1970s or earlier and prior to current stormwater requirements.
2412.purpose: The project is located in an older area that saw extensive flooding in Hurricanes Ian & Milton. It includes the construction of two new stormwater ponds, along with new pipes and inlets to route the stormwater to the new ponds, and the addition of a backflow prevention device to an existing outfall beneath the FEC railroad tracks. This will help relieve flooding for about 50 homes in the immediate area built mostly in the 1970s or earlier and prior to current stormwater requirements.
2412.activities: The improvements include constructing 2 stormwater ponds, new pipes and inlets to route the stormwater to the new ponds, and adding a backflow prevention device to an existing outfall beneath the FEC railroad tracks.
2412.direct_services: Adding stormwater storage via two new ponds in an old area built in the 1970s before modern stormwater requirements will help reduce flooding of structures, especially during hurricanes and severe rain events.
2412.population: The target population is approximately 50 residences that flooded during Hurricanes Ian and Milton. However, we also believe hundreds more will experience less water intrusion due to less water moving toward the Nova Canal system which was inundated during these storms.
2412.outcome: Protection of the general public from the environmental hazards associated with flooding by reducing the flooding of structures. A comparison of the number of flooded structures before the project and after the project during similar storm events will be the method of measuring the success of the project.

2003.description: Habitat for Humanity of Greater Volusia County provides opportunity for affordable homeownership through construction and providing a zero-interest mortgage for each home built with local individuals and families who complete an objection application process. We have served the community since 1986 building homes and providing more than 200 families with zero-interest mortgages and well-constructed homes. Legacy Woods is our first development and will provide 40 homes for affordable homeownership at build-out. This project request is for the funding of the foundation, block work, and roof trusses for twenty homes in Phase 2. The request is for $400,000 for 20 homes. Local donations, grant monies and recycled mortgage payments will fund the match of $3,600,000 which is the balance of the funds needed to fully build the twenty homes. Approximately 65 individuals will immediately be served

The local funding request will provide 10% of the costs - paying for the site work, foundation, block work, and roof trusses. Local donors, private grant funding, and the recycled mortgage payments (HFH of GVC provides a zero-interest mortgage for every home we build as the Homeowners pay their monthly mortgage including property taxes and homeowner's in

Once approved for the affordable homeownership program, all Homeowner Candidates complete 300 sweat equity hours. Those hours are completed on the construction site of other homes, at our ReStore and at least 100 hours on the Homeowner Candidate's own home. All general contractor services will be provided. We are a proven affordable home builder

Completed new construction with energy saving features. All appliances are included. A zero-interest mortgage provided by HFH of GVC for no more than 30% of household income to ensure affordability for no more than 30 years. On-going support as they transition into home

Others work in the hospitality field, manufacturing, and for the local school board in paraprofessional and school bus driver positions. These are hard-working individuals whose income and financial situation would not qualify for a conventional loan. W

The expected benefits to the Habitat Homeowners are stable and secure homeownership that helps them to be successful at self- sufficiency. The assurance of knowing that your mortgage payment is based on no more than 30% of household income provides for peace of mind, a reduction in stress and an opportunity for the family to improve their quality of life as well as the future of their children. Children can focus on schoolwork at home and achieve greater academic success. 2007.description: Florida's school choice system only thrives when every family- regardless of school type- can rely on safe, secure learning environments. Upward Trend Academy seeks state funding to support and implement essential campus safety. Including fire alarm systems, fire sprinklers, perimeter fencing and campus wide video monitoring. Florida's school-safety legislation provides requirements, but private schools are not eligible for additional funding. This project ensures private- school students receive the same protection as their public school peers and supports the long term sustainability of school choice in Florida.
2007.purpose: The goal of this project is to ensure Upward Trend Academy meets Florida’s school-safety expectations by upgrading critical safety infrastructure, including perimeter fencing, a comprehensive video surveillance system, a modernized fire alarm system, and the installation of required fire sprinklers. Private schools must comply with many of the same safety mandates outlined in s. 1006.07, s. 1006.12, Florida Fire Prevention Code, and the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Act, but
2007.activities: Funds will support the installation of perimeter fencing to establish a secure, controlled single point of entry; a campus- wide video monitoring system; upgrades to the school’s fire alarm system; and the installation of fire sprinklers to meet Florida Fire Code requirements. These improvements ensure the school is equipped to prevent unauthorized access, detect and respond to emergencies, meet life-safety standards, and strengthen compliance with state school-safety legislation and fire-safety
2007.direct_services: This project supports Florida's school-choice priorities by ensuring private schools can sustain themselves while providing families the safe, compliant learning environments they expect and deserve. The project will provide a significantly safer educational environment by reducing security risks, improving emergency detection and response, and protecting students and staff from fire hazards. Enha
2007.population: The project serves over 80 K–12 students with disabilities and learning differences, along with more than 35 staff members. Families choosing private education through Florida’s school-choice programs also benefit, as enhanced safety measures increase parental confidence and access to secure learning environments.
2007.outcome: Expected outcomes include: • Full compliance with Florida school-safety and fire-safety requirements • Improved protection against fire hazards through modern alarms and sprinkler systems • Reduced risk of unauthorized campus access • Stronger active-assailant and emergency-response readiness

2005.description: Boys & Girls Clubs of Volusia/Flagler Counties respectfully requests $4 million in state capital improvement funding to renovate, modernize and bring into full safety compliance seven youth facilities that collectively serve nearly 2,000 children and teens each year. This investment will ensure every Club provides a safe, innovative, and future-ready workforce environment where young people can learn, lead, and thrive.
2005.purpose: Boys & Girls Clubs of Volusia/Flagler Counties respectfully requests $4 million in state capital improvement funding to renovate, modernize and bring into full safety compliance seven youth facilities that collectively serve nearly 2,000 children and teens each year. This investment will ensure every Club provides a safe, innovative, and future-ready workforce environment where young people can learn, lead, and thrive.
2005.activities: Though the request is for capital improvements, the upgraded facilities directly strengthen daily youth services. Renovations, safety enhancements, technology labs, and expanded spaces will support STEM, AI, arts, literacy, workforce programs, homework help, mentoring, and teen engagement in safe, modern environments.
2005.direct_services: The funding will provide essential youth services not offered elsewhere, filling critical gaps in safety, academic support, mentoring, STEM learning, and workforce readiness. Modernized facilities will expand capacity and deliver urgently needed after-school and summer programs for children and teens who have no other safe, affordable options.
2005.population: The project serves children and teens ages 6–18 throughout Volusia and Flagler Counties, with a focus on youth from low- to moderate-income households, Title I school zones, and families impacted by hurricane displacement or limited access to safe after-school care. With expanded facilities and increased capacity, BGCVFC expects to serve approximately 2,600 youth annually, an increase of about 600 additional young people each year.
2005.outcome: The project will expand youth capacity, enhance safety, and create modern program spaces that improve academic performance, STEM engagement, arts participation, and workforce readiness for young people across Volusia and Flagler Counties. Outcomes will be measured through Club attendance records, homework completion tracking, pre/post program assessments, participation logs for STEM and enrichment programs, behavior and safety reports, and annual BGCA-aligned impact surveys. These tools collectively track increases in academic success, skill development, and overall youth well-being.

2392.outcome: Mitigate flooding by increasing and enhancing the capacity of the existing stormwater pump stations (Biscayne Gardens Shores Pump Stations #3)—measured by decrease in flooding and reduction in the number of flood complaints received.

Project locations: Pump Station #1 - NE 109 Street & N. Bayshore Drive. Pump Station #2 - NE 110 Street & N. Bayshore Drive.

The pumps electrical and mechanical components will be upgraded, hardened, and elevated, and a standby generator will be added. 2387.description: Remediation of the flooding and roadway issues at NW 132nd Street (NW 27th Ave.- NW 30th Ave). These local roads flood during any minimum rain event which causes major safety hazards and nuisances. This project will construct new storm drainage including catch basis with baffles and will discharge into an infiltration system. This project also involves the rehabilitation, reconstruction and upgrade of the roadway.
2387.purpose: Remediation of the flooding and roadway issues at NW 132nd Street (NW 27th Ave.- NW 30th Ave). These local roads flood during any minimum rain event which causes major safety hazards and nuisances. This project will construct new storm drainage including catch basis with baffles and will discharge into an infiltration system. This project also involves the rehabilitation, reconstruction and upgrade of the roadway.
2387.activities: The funds will support several key activities and services, including roadway reconstruction; alteration of the horizontal and vertical geometry; water-main replacement; sewer force main improvements; installation of a exfiltration drainage system; installation of signs and pavement markings and traffic management.

Sewer backups are often from the sanitary sewer system, which takes on some storm water as a result of infiltration/inflow.

2387.outcome: Benefit: enhance and improve environment or fish and wildlife quality by increasing the development to decrease the pollutants that can help the environment and lost of fish.
